# Patterns

Musical time, as a value. A `PatPattern<A>` is a function from a span of cycles to the events inside it, so it is queried rather than stored, and a pattern that never repeats costs no more to hold than one that does. Time is kept as an exact rational (`PatQ`, `BigInteger` over `BigInteger`) all the way through the transforms and is only converted to seconds at the boundary where something has to be scheduled, which is why a third of a cycle survives `fast`, `rev` and `every` without drifting. The notation and much of the vocabulary is Tidal's — `pat("bd [hh hh] sd")`, `stack`, `jux`, `off`, `degradeBy`, the `|+|` operator family — but an atom here means whatever you want it to mean, not a sample name, which is what lets the same pattern drive a note process, a Field `Fn`, a set of signal-graph parameters or an arbitrary side effect. `Sequencing.kt` is the note-and-piano-roll layer patterns bridge into, and `BeatLaunch.kt` is `.onBeat { … }`, which holds any launchable value until the next musical boundary. [Patterns: writing rhythm as a function of time](../pattern_language.md) is the prose for all of it.

## BeatLaunch.kt { #beatlaunch-kt }

Quantised launching: `.onBeat(…)` holds any launchable value until the next boundary of a
[`PatClock`](patterns.md#patclock-kt-patclock)'s grid, and `waitForBeat(…)` is the same wait spelled as a suspend call for code
inside `frames { }` or `loop { }`.

A grid here is two numbers against a clock. `every` is the spacing, in that clock's units, and
`offset` slides the whole grid, so `every = 4, offset = 1` puts boundaries at 1, 5, 9 and so on.
`preroll` moves only the wake-up, not the boundary: waking a little early is how work that takes
time can still land on the beat, and the value reported back is always the boundary itself.

`.onBeat` is an extension on `T`, not on any launch type, so it wraps whatever it is given,
including a bundle built with `+`. It returns a [`BeatLaunchSpec`](patterns.md#beatlaunch-kt-beatlaunchspec), which does nothing on its own.
The handler registered at the bottom of this file recognises that spec when it arrives as a
box's last expression, waits, and then hands the value it was wrapping back to the normal launch
machinery. A bundle wrapped once therefore starts as a unit:

    (audio { saw * 0.05f } +
        pat("bd [hh hh] sd").respond(cps = 0.5) { event ->
            __m("pat").patHighlight(event)
        }).onBeat(every = 4, preroll = 0.02)

Because the wait runs as a job owned by the box, stopping the box before the boundary arrives
cancels the launch rather than deferring it.

A boundary the clock is already sitting on, within `1e-6` of a clock unit, counts as reached, so
`.onBeat` on the downbeat starts now rather than a full period later.

## BooleanNetworkSequencing.kt { #booleannetworksequencing-kt }

Gives a [`BooleanNetwork`](data.md#booleannetworks-kt-booleannetwork)'s states a duration, which is all it takes to read one as music.

[`BooleanNetwork`](data.md#booleannetworks-kt-booleannetwork) itself is untimed: it is a list of nodes whose update rules all fire at once,
and `step` takes one state vector to the next. Everything here is an extension on that class, so
the dependency runs one way only. Nothing in the network model knows about clocks, notes or
boxes, and the network can be built, explored and drawn without any of this.

A timed run is a [`BooleanNetworkStep`](patterns.md#booleannetworksequencing-kt-booleannetworkstep) per update: the state, the state before it, and a start
and duration in seconds. One node is one lane, indexed as the network indexes its nodes, and
[`BooleanTriggerMode`](patterns.md#booleannetworksequencing-kt-booleantriggermode) decides what counts as an event on a lane. Choosing the mode does most of
the musical work, because a node that stays on for six steps is six notes under `ACTIVE` and one
under `RISING_EDGE`.

There are three ways out, in increasing order of commitment:

- `scheduledSteps` and `scheduledDrivenSteps` hand back the raw timed states as an `Iterator`,
  for anything that wants to read the rhythm itself.
- `scheduledNotes` and `asNoteProcess` take a mapper from a step to [`ScheduledNote`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-schedulednote)s and give
  back an iterator or a [`NoteProcess`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-noteprocess), which is the same thing a hand-written sequence produces,
  so `notesBetween` and `pianoRollSvg` work on it unchanged.
- `respond` and `respondAhead` build a [`BooleanNetworkResponseSpec`](patterns.md#booleannetworksequencing-kt-booleannetworkresponsespec), which runs the network
  against a [`PatClock`](patterns.md#patclock-kt-patclock) in real time and calls back per step. Returning one from a box is what
  starts it.

The `Driven` half of each pair takes a [`BooleanNetworkStateDriver`](patterns.md#booleannetworksequencing-kt-booleannetworkstatedriver), a lambda that writes into the
state vector before the network reads it. The network then updates from the forced value as
though it had produced it, which is how an oscillator, a MIDI input or a second network gets to
be one of the lanes.

Leaving `steps` null makes every one of these iterators infinite. That is the right answer for a
responder and the wrong one for anything that collects, so pass a bound when you are building a
list.

## CaSoundDocs.kt { #casounddocs-kt }

A cellular automaton as a rhythm, by way of the pattern language's own inverse parser.

The route is four steps and each one belongs to a different part of Field: an elementary rule is
stepped by `alife_ca.kt`, one of its rows becomes a step mask, [`patCondense`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--patcondense) finds the shortest
mini-notation that plays that mask, and [`patRenderStereoDirt`](audio.md#dirtrender-kt--patrenderstereodirt) plays the notation from the pinned
Dirt-Samples subset.
So the sound is not "a sonification of a CA" in the loose sense. It is the CA's row, spelled as
something a musician would have typed, and then played.

The condenser earns its place in the middle of that: it is a **measurement**. A row with
structure gets a much shorter spelling than one without, so `CaBar.compression` separates rule
90's self-similar rows from rule 30's centre column. Neither ratio can exceed one, because the
search is never allowed to lose to the flat spelling and a flat spelling carries overhead that
any grouping saves, so the `rule30-hats` scene asserts the *ratio* between the two -- rule 30's
at least 1.4 times rule 90's -- rather than a floor on either. That gap is the difference between
the two scenes here, and you can hear it.

### Every scene has an oracle outside the CA

Rule 90 from a single seed is Pascal's triangle mod 2, so [`binomialParity`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt--binomialparity) computes what the
stepper should have produced without stepping anything, and [`gasketBar`](patterns.md#casounddocs-kt--casounddocs--gasketbar) checks the two against
each other before any sound is made. Row *n*'s population is exactly `2^popcount(n)`, which is
what [`gasketScale`](patterns.md#casounddocs-kt--casounddocs--gasketscale) turns into pitch, so the melody's note sequence is checkable digit by digit.
[`rule30Bar`](patterns.md#casounddocs-kt--casounddocs--rule30bar) has no such closed form, so what is asserted there is the negative: a population near
half, and a longest run short enough that the sequence has no long runs in it.

### What it does not do

No realtime engine, no audio device, no GPU, no Field window. The renders are deterministic, so a
committed `.wav` regenerates byte-stably, which is the contract `DOUGH_DSP_PLOT_GALLERY.md` sets
and [`PatSoundDocs`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt-patsounddocs) follows. Run as the `synth.ca.sound` FIELD_TEST, every scene renders to a
temporary directory and runs its own checks, and nothing committed is written. Pass an output
directory as `args[0]` to regenerate the page's `.wav`s.

## DrawnMorphDocs.kt { #drawnmorphdocs-kt }

The harness that renders the sound on `chain_drawn_morph.md` from two strokes in a document's
drawing.

[`DrawnMorphDocs`](patterns.md#drawnmorphdocs-kt-drawnmorphdocs) reads a circle and a heart back through `notation`, pairs their points and plays
the in-between cloud's size as pitch. It runs as the `synth.drawn.morph` FIELD_TEST.

## DrawnScoreDocs.kt { #drawnscoredocs-kt }

A drawn score, heard — the harness behind `public/docs/chain_drawn_score.md`.

The route is three parts of Field that were written without each other in mind. A box draws a
score into the document's drawing with `notation { drawnScore() }`: a frame, a piano roll of
rectangles, a glissando drawn as a pen stroke, a held note drawn as a level line, and a text
label. `notation.space("score", x = 0.0..8.0, y = 84.0..48.0)` reads that drawing back as eight
beats of MIDI pitch, [`interpret`](patterns.md#drawnscoredocs-kt--drawnscoredocs--interpret) decides what each event means as notes (the loop the page
shows), [`patTimed`](patterns.md#notationpatterns-kt--pattimed) makes those a [`PatPattern`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patpattern), and [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) plays the pattern offline
into a `.wav`. [`pentatonic`](patterns.md#drawnscoredocs-kt--drawnscoredocs--pentatonic) is the page's second reading of the same drawing.

Then the sound is taken back apart. [`listen`](patterns.md#drawnscoredocs-kt--drawnscoredocs--listen) finds the onsets in the rendered audio with
[`PatSoundDocs.onsetPeaks`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patsounddocs--onsetpeaks) and the pitch of each note with YIN ([`patF0Frames`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--patf0frames)), and holds both
against the notes read from the drawing — so the claim "the audio plays the score" is a
measurement with an error in milliseconds and in semitones, not a caption.

[`renderWav`](patterns.md#drawnscoredocs-kt--drawnscoredocs--renderwav) needs no Field window and no browser: it opens an ephemeral document of its own,
draws the score into its drawing with the same `notation { }` code a box uses, and reads it
back through the same `NotationSpace`. As the `synth.drawn.score` FIELD_TEST everything renders
to a temporary directory and nothing committed is written.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DrawnScoreDocs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DrawnScoreDocs/)

**Used in:** [A Drawn Score, Heard](../chain_drawn_score.md)

## HeadTrackedSpatial.kt { #headtrackedspatial-kt }

The seam between a tracked head and [`patSpatial`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatial)'s listener.

The two halves of head-tracked binaural audio meet here and nowhere else:
[`OpenXRHmdTarget.headPose`](graphics.md#openxrhmdtarget-kt--openxrhmdtarget--headpose) reports where the wearer's head is, and [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom) renders a
pattern through Steam Audio's HRTF from wherever it is told the listener is. Between them sits
[`HeadPoseSource`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatial-kt-headposesource), an interface narrow enough that the audio side cannot tell an HMD from a
script.

### The conversion is a copy

OpenXR and Steam Audio use the **same** frame: right-handed, +X right, +Y up, -Z ahead, metres.
So `HeadPose.ofOpenXR` copies seven numbers and converts nothing. A handedness error between
these two frames leaves level, distance, occlusion and reverb all correct and silently swaps the
listener's ears. That is the failure [`afield.audio.spatial.steamaudio.World2D`](audio.md#geometry2d-kt-world2d) and
`World2DHandednessTest` guard against on the geometry side; `HeadTrackedSpatialSmokeTest` guards
this side of it, on rendered audio rather than on the paragraph above.

### Where to pump from

[`OpenXRHmdTarget`](graphics.md#openxrhmdtarget-kt-openxrhmdtarget)'s pose comes from `xrLocateViews` on the renderer's queue thread and is
published whole, once per frame, so the timer default is safe for it as for a [`StereoPoseSource`](graphics.md#stereoposesource-kt-stereoposesource)
(which latches by contract). Construct with `hz = 0.0` and call [`HeadTrackedListener.pump`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatial-kt--headtrackedlistener--pump) from
the frame callback only when the pose should change exactly on frame boundaries.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/HeadTrackedSpatial.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/HeadTrackedSpatial/)

## HeadTrackedSpatialSmokeTest.kt { #headtrackedspatialsmoketest-kt }

The listener half of `patSpatial`'s audio check: the pattern holds still and the head moves.

[`PatSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#patspatialsmoketest-kt-patspatialsmoketest) varies the tag and leaves the listener at the origin. Here the tag is fixed
and a head pose of the shape OpenXR reports drives the HRTF, over six cases: an identity pose
against no pose at all, a yaw, a step sideways, a walk towards the source, a tracking dropout,
and a [`VirtualHead`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatial-kt-virtualhead) on its own thread writing poses while the render thread reads them.

Nothing here is asserted against the wall clock. [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom)'s render loop has no pacing
beyond sleeping when its ring is at target fill, so a capture that drains the ring as fast as
blocks appear lets the whole chain free-run at whatever rate the machine allows. Every case
prints the factor it reached and none of them depends on it; [`PatSpatialBudgetProbe`](patterns.md#patspatialbudgetprobe-kt-patspatialbudgetprobe) owns the
timing questions.

Run it with `tools/run_field_tests.py --id synth.head-tracked-spatial.smoke`.

## LambdaSoundDocs.kt { #lambdasounddocs-kt }

A λ-term's *reduction* as a rhythm — the schedule, not the answer.

The route is four steps in four parts of Field that do not know about each other.
`afield.lang.lambda.lambdaterms` parses and compiles a term to an interaction net,
`afield.data.graph.interactionnets` reduces that net one reaction at a time, this file records each
reaction as a [`Beat`](patterns.md#lambdasounddocs-kt--lambdasounddocs--beat), and [`patCondense`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--patcondense), the mini-notation parser run backwards, finds the
shortest notation that plays the resulting step mask. [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) plays it.

### What this measures

`stdlib.lambda-terms.property` established on 2026-09-19 that the **answer** does not depend on
the scheduler, over 17 200 (term, scheduler) checks. It says nothing about the **route** taken to
reach it, which is what a trace records. So the measurement is the pair:

 * the normal form, which is the same under every [`ActivationOrder`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-activationorder) the harness runs, and
 * the step count, the rule sequence, the β mask and its condensation, which are not.

[`patCondense`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--patcondense) earns its place for the same reason it does in [`CaSoundDocs`](patterns.md#casounddocs-kt-casounddocs): it is a
**measurement**. A schedule whose β-steps fall into a figure gets a short spelling; one that
scatters them gets a long one. `Trace.betaCompression` is therefore a number about a *scheduler*
rather than about a term.

### The oracles

Every trace is checked against something outside the trace before it is allowed to make a sound:

 * `Trace.result` is asserted α-equivalent to [`LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder`](visualization.md#lambdaterms-kt--lambdaterms--referencenormalorder), the plain
   capture-avoiding evaluator, and equal across every order in [`ORDERS`](patterns.md#lambdasounddocs-kt--lambdasounddocs--orders).
 * every [`Beat`](patterns.md#lambdasounddocs-kt--lambdasounddocs--beat) carries at least one event, and every event kind is one of the six
   [`Lambda.rules`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--lambda--rules) declares — so [`EVENT_KINDS`](patterns.md#lambdasounddocs-kt--lambdasounddocs--event-kinds) is checked against the rule book rather than
   trusted.
 * the β count is asserted **constant across schedulers** while the total is not: see
   [`betaIsScheduleInvariant`](patterns.md#lambdasounddocs-kt--lambdasounddocs--betaisscheduleinvariant).

### What it does not do

No realtime engine, no audio device, no GPU, no Field window, and no layout:
`relaxIterations = 0` throughout, because the force-directed layout is `O(n²)` per iteration and
a reduction nobody is watching should not pay for a picture. The renders are deterministic, so a
committed `.wav` regenerates byte-stably. As the `synth.lambda.sound` FIELD_TEST every scene
renders to a temp dir and nothing committed is written; pass an output directory as `args[0]` to
regenerate the page's `.wav`s.

## Marf.kt { #marf-kt }

Function generation over the pattern language: stored material, a trajectory that reads it, and
the timing of that traversal, kept as three separate patterns.

The idea is borrowed from the Buchla 248 Multiple Arbitrary Function Generator, and the part worth
borrowing is not its step sequencer. It is the separation the 248 makes between

- the **material** stored in a bank of stages,
- the **address** that says which stage to read next,
- the **time** each stage is allowed to take,
- and the **continuous function** the generator draws while a stage is active.

On the hardware those are four patch points. Here they are four ordinary [`PatPattern`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patpattern)s, which is
the whole point: `slow`, `rev`, `every`, `euclid`, `degradeBy`, `randcat` and everything else in
TidalPatterns.kt / PatComposition.kt already work on all four, so this file adds almost no
combinators of its own. A reader is built from patterns and *is* a pattern: `signal()` hands back
a `PatPattern<Double>` in the sense of PatSignals.kt, and [`MarfReader.triggers`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfreader--triggers) hands back a
discrete `PatPattern<String>`. Both ends plug straight into `with(gain(...))`, `struct`,
`segment`, `respond` and the scheduler.

Read the surface from the outside in:

1. The four fields, patterned independently. Nothing here is a grid; the durations are real:

       val env = marf(
           value    = pat("<0 .7 .2 1>").nums(),
           duration = pat("<1 4 .25 2>").nums(),
           curve    = curves("<linear exp hold osc>"),
           fields   = MarfFieldClock.STAGES
       )

       env.at(3.5).value        // the continuous output, 3.5 cycles in
       env.at(3.5).stagePhase   // where inside its own stage that was

2. Stored material, read by a trajectory. Two readers, one bank, different journeys:

       val b = marfBank(
           rampTo(0.0), rampTo(0.3), holdAt(0.2), oscTo(0.9, cycles = 3), rampTo(0.8)
       )

       val a = b.read(pat("0 1 2 1 3 4").nums())
       val c = b.read(pat("0 2 4 1 3").nums().slow(3))
       val d = b.read(struct(euclid(5, 8), pat("0 4 2 3").nums()))

   The address is a pattern, so the trajectory is compositional material rather than a mode
   flag. `"<0 1 2 3 2 1>"` is ping-pong. `.every(4) { it.rev() }` is periodic reversal. There is
   no `direction = PINGPONG` in this file and there should never be one.

3. Out, as a signal or as pulses — the same temporal structure, both ways:

       pat("bd*8") with gain(a.signal().range(0.2, 1.0))   // continuous, into the algebra
       a.triggers().respond(cps = 1.0) { spawnParticles() } // discrete, one per stage

4. And the missing conversion, which is useful with or without a bank — an event stream read as
   a continuous function:

       pat("0 .5 1 .25").nums().hold()             // sample and hold
       pat("0 .5 1 .25").nums().ramp()             // linear between onsets
       pat("0 .5 1 .25").nums().interp(MarfCurve.Smooth)

### Where a stage's numbers come from

Stage `k` begins at an exact cycle instant `Tₖ`, and **every field is sampled at `Tₖ`** — value,
duration, curve, trigger, address, speed — through [`patSampleOver`](patterns.md#patalgebra-kt--patsampleover), the same latch the parameter
algebra uses for `gain(...)` at a note onset. Then `Tₖ₊₁ = Tₖ + durationₖ`.

A field pattern with **rests** holds rather than resets. If nothing is sounding at `Tₖ` — a
`struct(euclid(5, 8), …)` address on an off step, a `degradeBy` that dropped this one — the field
keeps the value the previous stage had. That is what a sample-and-hold does, and it is what makes
the thinning operators mean something on an address: `struct` and `degradeBy` become *how long an
address is held for*, rather than "and now, silently, address zero".

That recurrence is why this is not a sequencer: the reader's own traversal generates its clock,
so the duration pattern is consulted at instants the duration pattern chose. Give four values a
`"<1 4 .25 2>"` duration and you get

    |--0--|--------.7--------|-.2-|----1----|

rather than four equal steps. Give the address a period of 6 and the duration a period of 4 and
the two drift against each other with a period of 12 — which is the whole reason to keep them
apart.

There is one real choice buried in "sampled at `Tₖ`", and [`MarfFieldClock`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marffieldclock) is where it lives.
Reading the fields at the wall-clock instant `Tₖ` (`CYCLES`) is the hardware answer
and never fails silently: every pattern says something at every instant. Reading them at cycle
`k` instead (`STAGES`) makes the fields a per-stage *sequence*, so `duration = "<1 4 .25 2>"`
gives stages of exactly those four lengths and `address = "<0 1 2 1 3 4>"` walks the bank one
slot per stage no matter how long a stage takes. In `STAGES` one cycle of a field pattern is one
stage, so a bare `"0 .7 .2 1"` has three steps the clock cannot see — and rather than collapse to
`0`, that is now **refused at construction, by field name**. See `marfCheckFieldClock`.

`STEPS` is the third reading and the one that means what a sub-cycle field looks like it means:
it subdivides each cycle of `STAGES`, so a field contributes one stage per onset and at least one
per cycle. `address = "<0 3> 1"` is then the three-entry sequence `0, 1, 3, 1` rather than an
error. `STEPS` and `STAGES` agree exactly on every pattern with at most one onset per cycle, so
`<…>`, `slow(3)` and a signal read identically in both.

Only a stack is beyond all three. `"<0 3>, 1"` puts two layers on one instant, a field latches to
one value, and no choice of clock recovers the other — so that too is refused in the sequence
readings rather than half-read.

Accumulation is exact. Durations arriving as `Double` are taken to [`PatQ`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patq) at
[`MARF_DURATION_DENOM`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marf-duration-denom) resolution, so a reader is still phase-locked to the bar after ten
thousand stages; a `Double` accumulator would not be. A duration is floored at
[`MARF_MIN_DURATION`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marf-min-duration) so that a zero or negative sample cannot stall the walk.

Sampling a *continuous* field pattern needs an arc rather than an instant, and the probe used is
`[Tₖ, Tₖ + 1/65536)`, so `duration = sine().range(0.25, 2.0)` reads the sine essentially at the
stage boundary. A discrete field pattern is unaffected by the probe width: the latch picks the
event containing `Tₖ` however finely the source is subdivided.

### Local time

[`MarfSample`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marfsample) is the temporal context, and the reason it exists is that several notions of time
are live at once. `cycle` is the global coordinate, `stageIndex` counts stages, `stageTime` is
cycles since this stage began and `stagePhase` is that normalised to `0..1`. A curve is written
against `stagePhase` and never has to reconstruct it:

       MarfCurve.Shape("chirp") { p -> 0.5 + 0.5 * kotlin.math.sin(p * p * 40.0) }

The analogy worth keeping is a shader. A fragment shader computes over `uv`; a stage computes
over `stagePhase`, inside a structure the pattern algebra laid out.

### Continuous address

The address is a `PatPattern<Double>`, not a `PatPattern<Int>`, and a fractional address blends.
At address `1.35` the reader evaluates stages 1 and 2 over the same local phase and mixes the
outputs `(1-α)·f₁(p) + α·f₂(p)` with `α = 0.35`, blending their durations the same way. So

       b.read(sine().range(0.0, 4.0))

glides through the bank instead of stepping through it, and the bank stops being five slots and
starts being a sampled one-dimensional family of functions. The entry value is shared between
the blended components, so the output stays continuous across a stage boundary exactly as it
does for an integer address.

There is a catch, and it is arithmetic rather than a bug. A periodic address is **latched once
per stage**, so a reader with periodic durations visits exactly

    lcm(address period, stage period) / stage period

distinct addresses and then repeats forever. `sine().range(0, 4)` against quarter-cycle stages is
four of them — the address cycles `2, 4, 2, 0, 2, 4, 2, 0, …` and the "glide" is a four-step
sequencer wearing a signal's clothes. `sine().slow(3)` is twelve, which is better and still a
sequence. What actually reads as a glide is a long count: `saw().slow(8)` against those stages is
thirty-two, and an aperiodic address (`perlin()`, `rand()`) never repeats at all. No exception is
raised in any of these cases, so the symptom is what you hear rather than what you read.

Count the distinct [`MarfSample.address`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfsample--address) values **rounded** when you check. An aliased address
repeats to a few parts in 10⁴ rather than bit-exactly, because the probe instant is an exact
rational and `PatQ.toDouble()` rounds it at twelve places — a raw `distinct()` reports seventeen
different addresses for the four-value cycle above. `MarfSmokeTest` prints both cases.

### Values other than numbers

A stage's value is a type parameter, and [`MarfSpace`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marfspace) is the arithmetic a reader needs to move
one value toward another: [`MarfSpace.sub`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfspace--sub) for the direction, [`MarfSpace.scale`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfspace--scale) to walk part of
it, [`MarfSpace.add`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfspace--add) to arrive. The curve stays scalar, because a stage's shape is
one-dimensional however many dimensions its value has.

       val path = marfBankIn(
           MarfVector3f,
           stageTo(Vector3f(0f, 0f, 0f), 1.0),
           stageTo(Vector3f(1f, 0.5f, 0f), 0.5, MarfCurve.Smooth)
       ).read(pat("<0 1>").nums(), fields = MarfFieldClock.STAGES)

       path.at(1.5).value               // a Vector3f
       path.signal { it.x.toDouble() }  // any component, as an ordinary signal

`marf(...)` and `marfBank(...)` are the scalar spellings and give a `MarfReader<Double>`;
[`marfIn`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfin) and [`marfBankIn`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfbankin) take a space. Instances for Field's generated linalg vectors are in
MarfVectors.kt, and they copy before they write — the in-place `add`/`mul`/`normalize` members
would rewrite the bank's own stage targets rather than produce one wrong frame.

[`MarfSpace`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marfspace) is a vector space, which rules out the types that are not one: a quaternion
interpolates by `slerp` and a hue wraps, so neither is `add`/`scale` and neither has an instance.
Those want a reader whose blend is its own function.

### Nesting a pattern inside a stage

A stage's continuous behaviour is a [`MarfCurve`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marfcurve), and `MarfCurve.Shape` can close over anything,
including another reader. What is not modelled is a nested pattern with a local temporal scope
of its own: `stagePhase` reaches a `Shape` as a `Double`, so a pattern read in there has no
evaluation context to be slowed, reversed or thinned in.

## MarfGallery.kt { #marfgallery-kt }

Headless **figure gallery** for the function-generation layer in `Marf.kt`, and the check that
every figure on `marf.md` is a measurement of the reader it claims to draw.

Output is **SVG**, like the piano rolls in `PatPianoRollGallery.kt` and for the same reason: a
stage plot is line art, so drawing it as vector geometry makes it diffable — a changed curve is a
changed polyline in the file rather than a changed PNG blob. No AWT, no browser, no GPU, no Field
window.

A MARF figure is not a piano roll, which is why it has its own renderer. A roll draws events; a
reader has a *continuous output* and a *stage structure*, and what a figure has to show is how the
two relate. So a reader's lane draws four things at one shared time scale:

- the **output**, as a polyline densely sampled through [`MarfReader.at`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfreader--at);
- the **stage boundaries**, as dashed verticals, one per stage the reader actually entered;
- the **address** in force during each stage, printed in the stage's own span (`~` when the
  address fell between two slots);
- a **pulse** tick where the stage emitted one, taken from [`MarfReader.triggers`](patterns.md#marf-kt--marfreader--triggers).

Reading down a column therefore compares the same instant across every lane, and a figure with
three lanes over one bank is the architecture's whole claim in one picture. A lane may also hold a
plain signal rather than a reader — that is how the `hold` / `ramp` / `interp` figure is drawn,
since those conversions produce signals and have no stages to show.

### What every figure guarantees

Every figure is drawn from the readers it claims to draw and held to them: one boundary vertical
per stage, one polyline point per sample, one pulse tick per triggering stage, no stage starting
past the plotted window, and no non-finite output. So a figure can neither invent a stage nor
lose one.

Two of those properties are about the layer rather than the drawing:

- **the output is continuous across every interior stage boundary whose arriving stage does not
  step** — exactly, comparing the departing stage's value at phase 1 against the arriving stage's
  at phase 0, with no tolerance. This is what makes a bank of stages an envelope generator rather
  than a list of disconnected ramps, and it is invisible at the resolution the figure draws. A
  stage steps exactly when its curve's shape is non-zero at phase 0, which is what `hold` is, so
  those boundaries are skipped by that test rather than by hand;
- **a figure whose point is that two readers differ really does draw two different curves**, so
  "one bank, three journeys" cannot become three copies of one journey.

Each figure then runs its own `verify` over the stages it drew, which is where the specific claim
lives — that the patterned durations really are 1, 4, ¼ and 2 cycles exactly; that
`every(4) { rev() }` reverses the first cycle's addresses and leaves the next three; that a rest
in a euclidean address holds the previous slot rather than snapping to zero.

Run the lot with `tools/run_field_tests.py --id synth.marf.gallery`; every figure renders to a
temp dir and nothing committed is written. Pass an output dir as `args[0]` (or set
`MARF_FIGURE_DIR`) to regenerate the committed figures under `public/docs/assets/marf/`.

Add a figure by appending one [`Figure`](patterns.md#marfgallery-kt--marfgallery--figure) to [`FIGURES`](patterns.md#marfgallery-kt--marfgallery--figures); `MarfDocsGuardTest` then requires
`public/docs/marf.md` to reference it, and requires every committed SVG to belong to one.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/MarfGallery.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/MarfGallery/)

## MarfSmokeTest.kt { #marfsmoketest-kt }

The worked example for `Marf.kt`, and the check that it holds together: one bank, several
readers, and what each reader is doing printed as text.

`main` prints five rows per reader — current address, current stage, stage phase, generated
value and stage-boundary pulses — for two readers over shared material, then swaps
`every(4) { rev() }` into one reader's address and prints them again. Content, timing, addressing
and interpolation are separate, so transforming one reader's address cannot disturb the other and
cannot alter the bank; the run checks both.

The transform itself only bites on an address with steps inside the cycle: on a `<…>`
address, which holds one event per cycle, `rev()` has nothing to reverse, so the run repeats the
comparison over four stages a cycle and asserts that cycle 0 comes out reversed and cycle 1 does
not.

### The livecoding version

The same patch in a box, driving sound. `marfBank` is the material; the three readers are three
journeys through it; nothing about the bank knows it is being read three times:

    val b = marfBank(
        rampTo(0.1, 1.0), rampTo(0.9, 0.5), holdAt(0.4, 2.0),
        oscTo(0.7, 1.0, cycles = 3.0), curveTo(0.2, 0.25, amount = 4.0)
    )

    val slowArc  = b.read(pat("<0 1 2 1 3 4>").nums(), name = "arc")
    val fastArc  = b.read(pat("<0 2 4 1 3>").nums().slow(3), speed = constant(4.0), name = "fast")
    val glide    = b.read(sine().range(0.0, 4.0), duration = constant(0.25), name = "glide")

    // Continuous out: three readers of one bank as three parameters of one voice.
    val voice = pat("bd*8")
        .with(gain(fastArc.signal().range(0.25, 1.0)))
        .with(pan(glide.signal()))
        .with(speed(slowArc.signal().range(0.5, 2.0)))

    voice.respond(cps = 1.0) { patVoice(it) }

    // Discrete out, from the same temporal structure: one pulse per stage.
    slowArc.triggers().respond(cps = 1.0) { println("stage ${it.value}") }

Then change one line and nothing else:

    val slowArc = b.read(pat("<0 1 2 1 3 4>").nums().every(4) { it.rev() })   // periodic reversal
    val slowArc = b.read(struct(euclid(5, 8), pat("0 4 2 3").nums()))         // euclidean trajectory
    val slowArc = b.read(sine().range(0.0, 5.0))                              // glide, not step

### The graphics version

Driving geometry shows the architecture more directly than driving notes does. Three readers
share one bank and become three coordinates, so the shapes are related without being
synchronised:

    val x = b.read(pat("<0 1 2 3 4>").nums(), name = "x")
    val y = b.read(pat("<0 2 4 1 3>").nums().slow(3), name = "y")
    val r = b.read(sine().range(0.0, 4.0), duration = constant(0.5), name = "r")

    frames {
        val t = musicClock().now
        val p = vec2(x.atSeconds(t).value, y.atSeconds(t).value) * 400.0
        ln.clear().circle(p, 10.0 + 60.0 * r.atSeconds(t).value)
    }

A `frames { }` block needs a renderer to tick at all, so that last one belongs in a box with a
graphics parent rather than here, which stays headless.

## MarfVectors.kt { #marfvectors-kt }

[`MarfSpace`](patterns.md#marf-kt-marfspace) instances for Field's generated linalg vectors, so a reader can emit a position, a
colour or a set of material parameters instead of one number.

Everything in `Marf.kt` is generic over the value type already; this file supplies the arithmetic
for the three types most stage material actually is. The reason it is a file of its own is the
dependency direction: the core layer needs nothing but `PatPattern`, and keeping `afield.math.linalg`
out of it means a reader over some other type costs one object rather than an edit to the layer.

    val trajectory = marfBankIn(
        MarfVector3f,
        stageTo(Vector3f(0f, 0f, 0f), 1.0),
        stageTo(Vector3f(1f, 0.5f, 0f), 0.5, MarfCurve.Smooth),
        stageTo(Vector3f(0f, 1f, 1f), 2.0, MarfCurve.Exp(3.0))
    )

    val path = trajectory.read(pat("<0 1 2>").nums(), fields = MarfFieldClock.STAGES)

    path.at(3.5).value              // a Vector3f
    path.signal { it.x.toDouble() } // and any component as an ordinary signal

### Every instance copies before it writes

This matters more here than the arithmetic does. In `afield.math.linalg`, `add(other)`,
`mul(scalar)`, `sub(other)` and `normalize()` are **in-place members** that return the receiver,
and `/` resolves to the mutating member operator rather than to the allocating extension. A stage
target lives in a bank and is read once per stage for as long as the reader runs, so a single
in-place write would corrupt the material rather than produce a wrong frame:

    a.add(b)                // WRONG: mutates a, which is the bank's stored target
    a.add(b, Vector3f())    // right: fresh destination, a and b untouched

Every method below uses the out-parameter form. `MarfVectorSpaceTest` reads a bank twice and
requires the second pass to agree with the first, which is the property that a mutating
implementation breaks and a type check does not.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/MarfVectors.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/MarfVectors/)

One note of a [`patTimed`](patterns.md#notationpatterns-kt--pattimed) pattern: it sounds from `start` to `end`, in beats from the start of the cycle, at MIDI `note` (fractional notes are microtones), with [`gain`](patterns.md#patalgebra-kt--gain) 0..1.

One note a drawn score plays: `start` and `end` in the space's x units, `pitch` in its y units. [`gain`](patterns.md#patalgebra-kt--gain) is the pen pressure where the mark recorded one (0..1), else null.

## Orca.kt { #orca-kt }

ORCA, the two-dimensional livecoding sequencer, running in a box output with its notes, control changes, UDP and OSC
messages delivered to Kotlin callbacks; start it with [`orca`](patterns.md#orca-kt--orca).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Orca.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Orca/)

**Used in:** [ORCA](../orca.md)

## PatAlgebra.kt { #patalgebra-kt }

The parameter-application algebra: combining patterns of different types, and choosing
whose rhythm survives.

This is the piece that turns the event language in TidalPatterns.kt into a composition
language. Everything else — signals, scales, chords, `off`, `jux` — is built on top of the
three combinators here.

Read the surface from the outside in:

1. Structure choice. When two patterns meet, one of three things can happen to the rhythm:

       pat("0 1").nums() `|+|` pat("10 20 30").nums()   // structure from BOTH: 4 events
       pat("0 1").nums() `|+`  pat("10 20 30").nums()   // structure from LEFT:  2 events
       pat("0 1").nums() `+|`  pat("10 20 30").nums()   // structure from RIGHT: 3 events

   The bars mark where the structure comes from, exactly as in Tidal. Every operator also has
   a prose alias (`addBoth`, `addLeft`, `addRight`) for people who dislike backticks.

2. Taking a value rather than combining:

       pat("bd sd") `#`  pat("a b c")   // left's rhythm, right's values (Tidal's `|>`)
       pat("bd sd") `|L` pat("a b c")   // left's rhythm, left's values  (Tidal's `|<`)

3. Named parameters, which is what you actually reach for:

       val voice = pat("bd sd hh sd") with gain(sine().range(0.3, 1.0)) with pan(saw())

   A parameter is stored in the event's existing `annotations` map, so it survives every
   transform in the language, arrives intact in `PatScheduledEvent`, and reads back typed:

       voice.peek(4).forEach { println(it.value to it.num("gain")) }

### Structure choice, precisely

- `appBoth` — the cross product of every pair of intersecting events; each output arc is the
  *intersection*. This is the only one of the three that can create events.

- `appLeft` — **exactly the left pattern's events survive**, one output per input. Each left
  event queries the right pattern over its own arc and takes the right event containing the
  left arc's start.

- `appRight` — the mirror image.

The "query the right over the left's arc, latch at the left's start" rule is the one place this
language knowingly diverges from Tidal, and the reason is the event type. Tidal splits the left event
into fragments, one per overlapping right event, because its events carry both a `whole` and a
`part`. `PatEvent` has a single arc, so fragmenting here would silently multiply notes: ask for
four kicks with a sixteen-step filter sweep and you would get sixty-four kicks. Instead:

- a **discrete** right pattern latches its value at note onset, which is what a synth voice
  does anyway (parameters are read when the envelope is triggered);
- a **continuous** right pattern answers the left event's whole arc with a single event whose
  value is the midpoint of that note, so `gain(sine())` gives one gain per note, taken at the
  middle of the note.

One implementation, both behaviours, and note count is preserved. `PatAlgebraTest` asserts the
cardinality laws and the midpoint sampling in exact rational cycle space.

Because `appLeft` never fragments, sub-cycle queries sample the *clipped* fragment's start.
Every scheduling path in the language (`eventSequence`, `scheduled`, `peek`) queries whole
cycles, so this only matters if you call `events(...)` with a partial arc by hand.

## PatClock.kt { #patclock-kt }

The transport everything scheduled in `afield.audio.synth` reads: one monotonic number that can be
paused, sought and subdivided, so that patterns, Boolean networks and audio launches share a
single notion of the current time.

A [`PatClock`](patterns.md#patclock-kt-patclock) reports that number as `now`, in the clock's own units. The shared clock advances
one unit per second of wall time, so a unit is a second until you say otherwise. There is no
tempo field: a faster grid comes from `subdivide`, which returns a child reading exactly `factor`
times its parent and following the parent's pauses and seeks.

The constructor is internal, so a box reaches a clock two ways. `musicClock()` returns the one
process-wide clock, built on first call. `Box.patClock` is an inherited property, and the
metaroot is given the shared clock when it is created, so a box reads whatever its nearest
ancestor holds. Assigning `patClock` writes locally, which puts that box and everything under it
on a different timeline and leaves the rest of the document on the old one.

Every scheduling entry point in this package spells its `clock` default the same way, the box's
inherited `patClock` and then the shared clock. The two `respond` families accept `null` there
instead, and their callback scope then measures time as seconds since the launch, which nothing
can pause or seek.

Each method synchronises on one lock and returns the clock, so a setup line reads as one
expression:

    val clock = musicClock().reset(started = true)
    val sixteenths = clock.subdivide(4.0, label = "16ths")

## PatComposition.kt { #patcomposition-kt }

Compositional structure: the transforms that build a piece out of a pattern, and the pitch
vocabulary — scales, named chords, and voice leading.

TidalPatterns.kt gives you one line of music and the means to vary it. PatAlgebra.kt lets two
lines meet. This file is what you reach for when you want *an arrangement*: the same material
displaced, superimposed, rotated, split across the stereo field, and spelled in a key.

Read the surface from the outside in:

1. Displace and layer:

       pat("bd ~ sd ~")
           .off(PatQ.of(1, 8)) { it with gain(0.4) }     // a ghost note an eighth later
           .superimpose { it.fast(2) }
           .jux { it.rev() }                              // left ear forward, right ear reversed

2. Rotate and hold:

       pat("a b c d").iter(4)      // cycle 0: a b c d, cycle 1: b c d a, …
       pat("a b c d").linger(PatQ.of(1, 2))   // just "a b", twice

3. Choose per cycle:

       randcat(pat("bd*4"), pat("bd sd"), pat("~ sd"))
       wrandcat(pat("bd*4") to 3.0, pat("~ sd") to 1.0)
       pat("a b c d").shuffle(4)

4. Spell it in a key:

       run(8).scale("minor", root = 60)                   // eight degrees of C minor
       pat("0 3 4 3").nums().scale("dorian", root = 62)

5. Chords, and the part Tidal has no answer for — voice leading:

       val progression = chords("c'maj7 a'min7 d'min7 g'dom7")
       progression.voiceLead(center = 60).notesOf()

   `voiceLead` picks each chord's inversion and octave to minimise the total semitone movement
   of the voices from the previous chord, which for that progression is close to an order of
   magnitude less than playing the chords from their roots. The harmony survives it: every chord
   comes back as the same set of pitch classes, in the same number of voices, inside the register
   asked for. `PatCompositionTest` asserts those three and that the movement strictly decreases,
   and prints the before-and-after figures rather than pinning them.

## PatCondense.kt { #patcondense-kt }

The shortest mini-notation expression that plays a given rhythm.

`PatTranscription.kt` writes a rhythm out flat: [`patNotationOf`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--patnotationof) fits a step grid to a set of onsets
and emits one slot per step, `x . . x . . x .`, which is faithful and says nothing about what it is
looking at. `bd(3,8)` says the same thing in a third of the characters and names the figure.

This file gets from the first spelling to the second. Give it a rhythm, as a mask, a `PatPattern`, a
list of events or a [`PatTranscription`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt-pattranscription), and it returns the shortest string in Field's own
mini-notation whose parse renders to an **identical** event set, together with the structure it
found.

**Description length is the whole criterion.** There is no notion here of a "better" reading of a
rhythm than a shorter one. `x ~ ~ x ~ ~ x ~` is `x(3,8)` because that is six characters against
fifteen, not because Euclidean rhythms are privileged, and a figure that no operator shortens
comes back as itself, spelled out. `PatCondenseTest` asserts that last part over generated
structureless masks, since a condenser that always found *something* would be finding nothing.

**The oracle is Field's own parser.** Every candidate this file emits is handed back to [`pat`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt--pat), the
same entry point a box calls, re-rendered, and compared event for event against the target. Nothing
is accepted on the strength of the reasoning that produced it, and there is no second hand-written
evaluator to drift away from the language. The proposers below are allowed to be wrong, because
being wrong only costs a rejected candidate.

**What it searches.** The candidate grammar is read off `MiniPat.Node` (`TidalPatterns.kt:1127`) —
what the parser actually accepts, not what a mini-notation tutorial says. Atoms and `~`; `_` holds
and their `@n` spelling; `[ … ]` grouping at every divisor of the span; `x!n` replication; `x*n`
repetition; `X(p,s,r)` Euclidean figures and `X(kN)` / `X(gN)` Kolakoski ones over any repeated
*term* rather than only a repeated atom; `a, b` stacking, from an interval partition of overlapping
events; and `< … >` alternation when the cycles differ. What it does **not** search is listed in
`dev_docs/PAT_CONDENSE.md` and pinned as tests, so the list cannot go stale on its own.

**It is bounded, and it says so.** A structural search over this grammar does not terminate if you
let it enumerate freely, so the range DP keeps [`PAT_CONDENSE_BEAM`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--pat-condense-beam) candidates per span, stops
proposing after [`PAT_CONDENSE_NODES`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--pat-condense-nodes) spans, refuses a grid finer than [`PAT_CONDENSE_MAX_SLOTS`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--pat-condense-max-slots)
steps, and calls the oracle at most [`PAT_CONDENSE_ORACLE_CALLS`](patterns.md#patcondense-kt--pat-condense-oracle-calls) times. Every one of those bounds is
reported on the result, so a caller can tell a genuine "there is nothing shorter" from a search that
ran out of room.

## PatFunctions.kt { #patfunctions-kt }

Bridge from `pat(...)` into scalar functions (`Functions.Fn`).

Three surfaces, in increasing order of how late the numbers arrive:

1. String atoms:

     val fn = pat("g:(0,0.12) tent:(1,0.08,0.8) adsr:(0.6,0.01,0.08,0.4,0.2)")
         .asFn(cps = 2.0, range = 0.9)

2. Typed atoms with late-bound values:

     val fn = pat("a b c") { atom ->
         when (atom) {
             "a" -> gaussianAtom(sigma = 0.08) { x -> kotlin.math.sin(local(x) * 12.0) }
             "b" -> gaussianAtom(sigma = 0.12) { x -> bipolarRandom() * (1.0 - normalized(x)) }
             else -> adsrAtom(attack = 0.01, decay = 0.08, sustain = 0.4, release = 0.2) { x ->
                 0.5 + 0.5 * noise(x, frequency = 18.0)
             }
         }
     }.asFn(cps = 2.0, maxLookAhead = 0.5)

The evaluator keeps a rolling cache of decoded atoms and only unrolls the
source pattern far enough ahead to cover the maximum possible pre-support of
future atoms. The current string forms are:

- `g:(value,sigma[,weight])`
- `tent:(value,radius[,weight])`
- `box:(value,radius[,weight])`
- `wendland:(value,radius[,weight])`
- `spline:(value,radius[,weight])`
- `env:(value,attack,release[,weight])`
- `adsr:(value,attack,decay,sustain,release[,weight])`

3. String atoms with `%binding` placeholders resolved at event-decode time:

     var t = 0.0
     val fn = pat("g:(%x,0.2) tent:(0.3,0.08,0.8) adsr:(%y,0.01,0.08,0.4,0.2)")
         .asFn(cps = 2.0, range = 0.9) { binding ->
             when (binding) {
                 "x" -> Math.random()
                 "y" -> Math.sin(t)
                 else -> 0.0
             }
         }

   Any numeric position in a string atom can hold `%name` instead of a literal.
   The resolver is called at event-decode time (when the evaluator unrolls
   events), so each cycle gets a fresh snapshot of the bound values.

   If no explicit resolver is given, `%name` bindings are resolved from the
   current box's KotlinInterface vars table (`Box.context` → `ki.context.vars`).
   Any `Number`-typed var is coerced to `Double`; non-numeric or missing vars
   resolve to `0.0`.

### The `pat` graph op

A string-atom pattern does not just *evaluate* as an `Fn`, it appears in the
`Fn` graph as a node of its own — `op = "pat"` — so a rhythm is a first-class
citizen of the rewrite/fit/evolve machinery rather than an opaque lambda that
happens to produce numbers. See `scanPatAtomSlots` for what gets hoisted.

- `strings["source"]` is the pattern text, with the node's *current* numbers
  spliced back in, so a fitted gesture is a string you can paste into a box.
- every numeric position of every string atom becomes a role-tagged child
  (`atom0.sigma`, `atom1.attack`, …), and `cps` is one too. Those children are
  `param` leaves, which is exactly what `extractParameters` / `fitGradient`
  treat as θ — so Adam tunes kernel widths, atom values and tempo directly.
- `numbers` carries `range` and `outside`, and `booleans` carries `strict`.
  These describe the *evaluator* rather than the gesture, so they are kept
  out of θ: a gradient has no business wandering into a cache bound.

A parameter child is read at each atom's own onset rather than once at build
time, so grafting a real signal into a role (rather than leaving the constant
leaf there) gives a kernel width that drifts across the piece.

Not every pattern can carry the node. The ones that cannot fall back to an
opaque `Fn`, which evaluates identically and simply cannot be rewritten:

- the typed-atom and custom-`atomDecoder` surfaces (2. above) hold user
  lambdas, and a lambda cannot describe how to rebuild itself;
- a `%binding` in a numeric position resolves against live box state at
  decode time, so the result is not a function of `x` alone. `fitGradient`
  samples non-monotonically and would be fitting a moving target, so a source
  that really uses a binding stays opaque. A binding *resolver* that the text
  never calls on is harmless, and does not cost the node.

## PatKolakoski.kt { #patkolakoski-kt }

Kolakoski rhythms: a bar whose own run lengths are written into it.

`euclid(3, 8)` asks for the most even spread of three onsets over eight slots, and answers with a
density and a period you chose in advance. A Kolakoski rhythm answers a different question — what
does a bar look like when the lengths of its runs are the bar itself? — and keeps answering it,
one step at a time, for as many steps as you ask for.

The Kolakoski word over {1, 2} begins

    1 2 2 1 1 2 1 2 2 1 2 2 1 1 2 1 1 2 2 1 …

and it is the only sequence over {1, 2} starting with 1 that is its own run-length encoding: one
1, two 2s, two 1s, one 2, one 1, two 2s, … — reading the runs off gives 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, … back.
[`kolakoskiWord`](patterns.md#patkolakoski-kt--kolakoskiword) generates it; [`KolakoskiReading`](patterns.md#patkolakoski-kt-kolakoskireading) is the choice of how to hear it.

    kolakoski(16)                          // x..xx.x..x..xx.x   — runs, the self-describing one
    kolakoski(16, KolakoskiReading.GAPS)   // xx.x.xxx.xx.x.xx   — gaps between onsets

`RUNS` reads the terms as alternating on- and off-runs, starting with an on-run, so the rhythm's
own run lengths spell out the word that made it. `GAPS` reads each term as the distance to the
next onset, the way a Euclidean rhythm's onsets sit on a step grid. Every step is then either an
onset or a single rest, which fills in the long gaps the run-length reading leaves: eleven onsets
in sixteen steps against the other reading's eight.

Both readings are **prefix-stable**: the first sixteen steps of `kolakoski(32)` are exactly
`kolakoski(16)`. Turning the step count up extends the figure instead of re-placing it, so the
step count is a dial you can turn without the hits you already have jumping around. `euclid`
cannot do that, because the step count is part of the question it answers: `euclid(3, 8)` is
`x..x..x.`, and the first eight steps of `euclid(3, 16)` are `x....x..`. `PatKolakoskiTest`
asserts both halves of that contrast.

The alphabet is a parameter. `kolakoski(16, a = 2, b = 3)` is the self-describing word over
{2, 3} — 2 2 3 3 2 2 2 3 3 3 2 2 … — which has no run shorter than two, so that figure never
leaves a lone hit or a lone rest: the same self-description, in bigger blocks.

## PatMiniNotation.kt { #patmininotation-kt }

The **mini-notation catalogue**: the forms a `pat("…")` string can take, one entry each, with
the piano roll and the audio clip the documentation publishes under it.

A table of prose can say that `bd*4` is four times as fast, but it cannot show that
`{bd hh cp}%8` phases against the bar, or let you hear that `bd _ _ sd` and `bd@3 sd` are the
same rhythm. Each entry here renders a roll and a clip, so a reader can look at the notation and
listen to it instead of taking a gloss on trust.

### One list, four consumers

`EXAMPLES` is the single source of truth. The same list produces the committed SVG rolls, the
committed `.wav` clips, the checks below, and, through `markdownSection`, the page's own
markdown. So an example cannot appear in the prose without a figure, carry a roll that disagrees
with its audio, or drift out of the order the page teaches it in.
`PatMiniNotationDocsGuardTest.the page's mini-notation section is what the catalogue generates`
compares the committed region of `pattern_language.md` against a fresh render and fails on any
difference, so the page cannot be hand-edited back out of step. Adding a form to the notation
means appending one `Example`.

### What each entry is checked against

As a FIELD_TEST (`synth.pat.mini`) every entry is rendered to a temp dir and asserted, writing no
committed assets:

 * it parses, draws at least one event, and draws nothing outside its own plotted window;
 * the SVG holds exactly one rectangle per event plus one backdrop per lane plus one page
   background, so the figure cannot invent or drop a note;
 * where an entry declares a longhand equivalent, as `bd ! ! sd` does for `bd!3 sd`, the two are
   compared **arc for arc and value for value across every cycle**, which is the one claim in
   this file a reader cannot check by eye;
 * the clip renders, through the pinned Dirt-Samples one-shots, to a RIFF/WAVE file, non-silent
   and all-finite; nothing is heard that the pattern did not schedule, and the level rises at
   every time it strikes;
 * `checkAtomColorClaim` holds the instrument colours to the voice in both directions: two
   tokens drawn in different colours must get different sounds out of the drum map, and two
   tokens sharing a colour must share a voice, so the roll never draws a difference the ear
   cannot find;
 * and the entries that make a *specific* musical claim carry their own check to prove it: that
   `?` is deterministic, that `<>` changes per cycle, that `%8` phases.

Pass an output dir as `args[0]` (or set `PAT_MINI_DIR`) to regenerate the committed captures
under `public/docs/assets/pattern_language/mini/`. `--markdown` prints the page section instead.

## PatOnsetDetection.kt { #patonsetdetection-kt }

Where a rendered pattern's notes actually start, measured from the audio.

One detector, so that two renderers can be measured with the same instrument. Field renders a
pattern offline through `patRenderStereo`; Sonic Pi renders it through SuperCollider after
`SonicPiPatterns` lowers it. Either can be checked against the pattern's exact rational schedule,
and the comparison only means anything if the measuring device is shared, since two detectors tuned
separately would each agree with their own renderer.

The signal processing is ordinary: an energy envelope, half-wave rectified flux, a local-maximum
test and a refractory gap. That is adequate because the question is *when* rather than *what*, and
these are bare percussive trains with nothing else in the mix.

Two details decide whether the answer means anything.

**Resolution.** A flux peak in a 256-sample window can only say which *frame* something happened
in, and a measurement whose resolution is coarser than the error it is looking for reports zero
whatever the truth is. So every coarse hit is walked back to the first sample that crosses a
fraction of the local peak, and [`patDetectOnsetSamples`](patterns.md#patonsetdetection-kt--patdetectonsetsamples) returns *samples* rather than frames.

**The refractory gap, applied after refinement.** `bd_haus` has a secondary energy rise 129 ms into
its decay. A first-past-the-post refractory on the coarse stage reports that shoulder and
suppresses the real attack behind it, which reads as a timing error rather than the detection error
it is. So the gap is the pattern's own smallest interval, and deduplication happens after the
onsets are exact.

## PatPatternReturnValue.kt { #patpatternreturnvalue-kt }

The step between `pat("bd sd").respond { … }` and a pattern that is actually playing: the
return-value handler that recognises a [`PatResponseSpec`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patresponsespec) coming back from a box and runs it.

`respond` is a builder. It captures the pattern, the cycles-per-second, the clock and the
callback into a spec and returns, having started nothing. This file is the other half, and the
arrangement is what makes a responder behave like every other launchable value in Field: it runs
because the box's last expression is one, it can be bundled with `+`, it can be wrapped in
`.onBeat`, and stopping the box stops it.

The loop it runs is short, and three of its rules shape what a callback sees:

- **Events that share a start time go out together.** The iterator is drained into a bucket of
  events within a nanosecond of each other, the wait happens once, and then the whole bucket is
  dispatched. A chord is a chord rather than a queue of near-simultaneous notes.
- **Events already in the past are dropped, not played late.** An event whose start has gone by
  is skipped, which is how a pattern joined mid-flight, or one whose callback overran, catches
  up instead of falling further behind.
- **`ahead` shifts the callback, not the schedule.** The wait targets `start - ahead`, so a
  callback that has to buy latency somewhere else, a sample player with its own scheduling
  queue, gets the event early and still knows its real time from `event.start`.

Dispatch is on the run loop unless `dispatchOnMain = false`, so a callback may touch boxes,
properties and graphics without hopping threads itself.

## PatPianoRollGallery.kt { #patpianorollgallery-kt }

Headless **piano-roll gallery** for the pattern language, drawing the operators defined across
`TidalPatterns.kt`, `PatSignals.kt`, `PatAlgebra.kt` and `PatComposition.kt`.

Output is **SVG**, not raster. A piano roll is line art (rectangles, gridlines, a parameter
polyline), so it is drawn as vector geometry, built here as plain strings. That also makes it
diffable: a changed operator shows up as a changed rectangle in the file rather than as a
changed PNG blob. There is no AWT, no browser, no GPU, no Field window.

Every rectangle is a **scheduled event**. Each lane queries its pattern over the roll's cycles
through `PatPattern.events(...)`, and nothing is hand-placed; the only parts chosen by hand are
the colours and the mapping from cycle time to pixels.

### How a roll is read

A roll is a stack of horizontal lanes drawn at one shared time scale, so reading down a column
compares the same instant across all of them. Most rolls are built as a source lane with its
transforms underneath: `pat("a b c d")` on top, then `rev()`, `euclid(3,8)`, `iter(4)` and the
rest below it. Where a form is shorthand for a longhand spelling, the two are lanes of the same
roll and the check compares them event for event.

### What each roll is checked against

As a FIELD_TEST (`synth.pat.gallery`) every roll is rendered to a temp dir and asserted: each
lane draws at least one event, no event falls outside the window the roll plots, and the SVG
holds exactly one rectangle per event plus one backdrop per lane plus one page background, so
the figure can neither invent a note nor drop one. Each roll then runs its own `verify` over the
events it actually drew, which is where the musical claim lives: that `rev` reverses, that
`euclid(3,8)` puts three onsets on the eighth grid with gaps as even as 8/3 allows, that
`iter(4)` rotates by a step per cycle, that `shuffle(4)` is a permutation every cycle, and that
a continuous parameter takes the value of its curve at each note's own midpoint. It writes no
committed assets during the test. Pass an output dir as `args[0]` (or set `PAT_ROLL_DIR`) to
regenerate the committed captures under `dev_docs/assets/pat_gallery/`.

Add a roll by appending one `Roll` to `ROLLS`.

## PatPitchDetection.kt { #patpitchdetection-kt }

What pitch a rendered pattern is actually sounding, measured from the audio.

`PatOnsetDetection` answers *when*. This answers *what*, and the two are not the same question with
a different threshold. An energy detector reads the amplitude envelope, so it can only see a note
that begins with an attack; a pitch detector reads periodicity, so it can see a note that begins
while the previous one is still sounding at full level. That difference is not a nicety. `patVoice`
defaults to `sustain = 1.0` (`PatSoundDocs.kt:747`), which means the *default* render of a gapless
melodic sequence is one continuous tone with exactly one attack in it, and an energy detector cannot
segment it however it is tuned — not because it is badly configured but because the evidence it
consumes is not in the signal. [`patDetectPitchChangeSamples`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--patdetectpitchchangesamples) is the complement, and
`PatPitchTranscriptionTest` measures the pair on the same render so the claim is a number.

The estimator is YIN, the cumulative-mean-normalised difference function, computed directly in the
time domain. `Spectral.kt:26` has a real FFT and an autocorrelation could be had from it for less
arithmetic, but YIN's threshold and its aperiodicity confidence are both defined on the difference
function, so keeping those constants over an autocorrelation would be taking the numbers without
the derivation they come from. At these corpus sizes the direct form costs seconds.

Three things here decide what the detector can resolve.

**The window is derived from [`PAT_PITCH_MIN_HZ`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--pat-pitch-min-hz), not fixed.** YIN needs a frame at least twice the
longest period it is asked to consider, so the lowest pitch admitted sets the frame length, and the
frame length sets the time resolution. A detector told it might hear a 65 Hz note is looking through
a 50 ms window whatever it is actually listening to. So `minHz`/`maxHz` are the same kind of
parameter as `patDetectOnsetSamples`' `minGapSeconds`: the detector is told what register it is
allowed to resolve, and buys sharpness with that promise. Telling it the truth about a treble line
shortens its window fourfold; guessing wide costs time resolution and gains nothing, which is why
the register is an argument here rather than a constant.

**A frame's pitch belongs to the frame's centre, not its start.** A frame spans `window + tauMax`
samples, so attributing its estimate to the first of them would report a note as starting up to 50 ms
before it did. [`PatF0Frame.centerSample`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--patf0frame--centersample) is what every consumer here uses, and a detected pitch
change is then localised inside the frame it was noticed in by re-analysing with a window sized to
the *new* note's period — the same walk-back move `patDetectOnsetSamples` makes, for the same reason.

**Timbre is not polyphony, and the detector has to be able to tell them apart.** A sawtooth is a
stack of partials and a triad is a stack of partials; refusing everything harmonically rich would
make the refusal worthless. [`patHarmonicResidual`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--patharmonicresidual) measures the fraction of strong spectral peak
energy that does *not* sit near an integer multiple of the detected f0, which is near zero for any
single note of any timbre and large for a chord. A monophonic detector that reports it cannot name
a chord is telling the truth; one that picks the loudest note is not.

## PatSignals.kt { #patsignals-kt }

Continuous (signal) patterns, and the discretisers that turn them back into events.

`PatPattern` in TidalPatterns.kt is an *event* stream: query an arc, get back a list of
things that happened inside it. A **signal** is the limiting case of that: exactly one event per
query, spanning the whole arc, whose value is a function of time. It needs nothing new in the type
system, because a signal is a `PatPattern<Double>` that always answers, so every combinator in the
language already applies to it.

Read the surface from the outside in:

1. A continuous value:

       val lfo = sine()                 // 0..1, one cycle per pattern cycle
       val swept = saw().range(200, 4000)

2. Sample it — nothing plays a continuous pattern directly, you discretise it:

       val steps = sine().segment(8)     // exactly 8 events per cycle
       val grid  = struct(euclid(3, 8), pat("bd"))

3. Or hand it to the parameter algebra in PatAlgebra.kt, which samples it for you:

       pat("bd sd hh sd") with gain(sine().range(0.2, 1.0))

### The sampling convention

A continuous pattern queried with arc `a` returns one event spanning `a` whose value is
`f(mid(a))`, and `mid(a)` is the **exact rational midpoint** `(a.start + a.end) / 2` — the
conversion to `Double` happens only inside `f`. Three reasons this is the right convention:

- it is what Tidal does, so ear-knowledge transfers;
- the midpoint is the only choice under which `segment(n)` samples each segment at that
  segment's own centre, which makes `sine().segment(4)` symmetric about the cycle and stable
  under `rev()` — an asymmetric convention (start, or end) breaks both;
- it is total. Every arc, however small, has a value, so a continuous pattern can never be
  "missed" by a query the way a zero-width event could be.

`segment(n)` does not sample at the query arc's midpoint. It builds the `1/n` grid itself, samples
the source over each **whole** grid cell, and clips to the query arc only afterwards, so the values
you observe do not depend on how the caller chopped up the arc. `PatSignalsTest` asserts that.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/PatSignals.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/PatSignals/)

**Used in:** [A pattern as a function generator](../marf.md), [Patterns: writing rhythm as a function of time](../pattern_language.md), [Petri nets](../petri_nets.md)

## PatSoundDocs.kt { #patsounddocs-kt }

Headless **offline sound renderer** for the pattern language: the audible companion to
`PatPianoRollGallery`'s piano rolls, in the same harness shape as `DoughDspSoundDocs`.

Every scene schedules a pattern and runs its events through [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) with a
[`PatVoiceSpec`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt-patvoicespec) — one oscillator, one one-pole lowpass, one exponential-decay envelope — reading
each event's own `gain`, `pan`, `cutoff` and `sustain` annotations. There is no realtime engine,
no audio device, no GPU and no Field window, and the render is deterministic, so a committed
`.wav` regenerates byte-stably.

### A before and an after in one file

Several scenes splice two versions of one pattern together with `whenCycle({ it >= 2 })`: the
opening cycles play it without the operator under discussion and the closing cycles play the
same pattern with it, so the difference arrives in a single listen. Those scenes check their two
halves against each other, requiring the modulated half's level to vary by some multiple of the
flat half's, rather than against a remembered number, so retuning the voice leaves the check
meaningful.

### What each render is checked against

As a FIELD_TEST (`synth.pat.sound`) every scene is rendered to a temp dir and asserted: a
RIFF/WAVE header whose declared channel count, sample rate and data size agree with the bytes on
disk; a duration within a tenth of a second of what the scene's own cycle count and tempo imply;
peak and RMS inside bounds that catch silence and runaway level; and then each scene's own
`verify`, which is where the musical claim lives. Those range from counting onsets to checking
that the filter sweep brightens, that the voice-led chords sound the notes the pattern says, and
that `jux` decorrelates the two channels. It writes no committed assets during the test. Pass an
output dir as `args[0]` (or set `PAT_SOUND_DIR`) to regenerate the committed captures.

Add a sound by appending one `Scene` to `SCENES`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/PatSoundDocs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/PatSoundDocs/)

**Used in:** [A Drawn Score, Heard](../chain_drawn_score.md), [Sound: from a pattern to something you can hear](../sound.md), [A Drawn Morph, Heard](../chain_drawn_morph.md)

## PatSpatial.kt { #patspatial-kt }

A pattern placed in space: `pat(...)` -> [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) -> Steam Audio HRTF, in realtime.

Three subsystems that do not know about each other, joined by two coercions and one thread:

| | what it is | what this file asks of it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`PatPattern`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patpattern) | Tidal-style pattern language, polyphonic by construction | query a cycle, read the annotations |
| [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) | the Strudel/superdough wasm synth, 32 voices | one engine per spatial source |
| `afield.audio.spatial.steamaudio` | Steam Audio 4.8.1 over FFM | direct path plus HRTF, per source, per block |

### The tag is the spatial parameter

A pattern's named parameters ride on [`PatEvent.annotations`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt--patevent--annotations), and [`with`](patterns.md#patalgebra-kt--with) writes any key at all into
that map, so the pattern language needed no extension to describe where a sound is. Six keys are
read here and every other key is forwarded to Dough untouched:

| tag | means | default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spat` | which spatial source -- i.e. which Dough engine -- the event plays on | `"0"` |
| `az` | azimuth in degrees; 0 ahead, +90 to the right | 0 |
| `elev` | elevation in degrees; +90 overhead | 0 |
| `dist` | distance in metres | 1.5 |
| `occl` | occlusion, 0 clear to 1 fully blocked | 0 |
| `air` | 1 to apply air absorption over distance, 0 for none | 1 |

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
patSpatial(
    pat("bd ~ sd ~, hh*8").with(
        paramOf("spat", pat("<kit hats>")),
        param("az", sine().range(-70.0, 70.0)),
        param("dist", "1 3 1 6"),
    ),
    cps = 2.0,
)
```

Because `az` can take a *continuous* pattern, `sine()` sampled per event is a source that moves
between notes; and because the placement is held on the source rather than the note, the same
pattern's next event on that `spat` group moves the whole group. The tags do not decorate the
sound, they aim it.

### Why one Dough engine per source

Steam Audio spatialises a **mono** signal -- a direction is a property of a whole buffer.
[`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) mixes its 32 voices to stereo and `MAX_ORBITS` is 1, so there is no way to pull two
separable signals out of one engine. Hence one engine per `spat` group, which is also why `spat`
exists at all rather than every event getting its own position.

Two consequences:

- **A pattern's `pan` is overridden.** Every event is sent with `pan/0`, which puts all of that
  engine's energy in its left channel, and that channel *is* the mono source signal. Panning is
  lossless this way (no `0.5*(L+R)` summing) but `pan` as a musical parameter is gone: `az`
  replaces it, and it is a better parameter.
- **Note onsets quantise to a Dough block**, 128 frames or 2.9 ms at 44.1 kHz. Dough takes an
  event through `evaluate()` and applies it at the next `dsp()`, so unlike [`PatSynthBank`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthbank) -- which
  is sample-exact, and proves it by rendering bit-identically at four buffer sizes -- this path
  cannot place a note inside a block. That is a property of Dough's event API, not of the
  scheduler.

### Why Dough is not on the audio thread

`PatSynth` puts the pattern *query* on a feeder thread because querying allocates, and keeps
synthesis on the audio thread because Field's own voices are a fixed amount of float arithmetic.
Neither half of that argument survives here. [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) is GraalWasm: every block enters a
polyglot context, and the JIT and the collector get a say in how long that takes.

[`PatSpatialBudgetProbe`](patterns.md#patspatialbudgetprobe-kt-patspatialbudgetprobe) measures it, idle and under load; the percentiles are in
`dev_docs/PAT_SPATIAL_MEASUREMENTS.md`. The **median is flat** -- the arithmetic of four wasm
engines and eight Steam Audio effects is 4% of a block either way, so nothing here needs
optimising. The **tail moves by a factor of three** with load the audio thread has no say over. A
path whose median fits twenty-five times over and which still misses one block in a hundred is
not a path to shave down; it is one to decouple.

So [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom) renders on its own thread into [`PatSpatialRing`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialring), and the audio thread's entire
job is a bounded copy out of that ring. A ring holding more milliseconds than the worst stall
turns a dropout into a dip in [`PatSpatialRing.fill`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatialring--fill), and [`PatSpatialRing.underruns`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatialring--underruns) is the number
that says whether that held.

The one stall the ring cannot absorb is booting a [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine), at 130-500 ms. That is what
[`PatSpatialRoom.prescanCycles`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatialroom--prescancycles) exists for, and what [`PatSpatialRoom.lateSourceBoots`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatialroom--latesourceboots) counts when
a `spat` tag turns up too late to have been prescanned.

### What limits the render thread

Not the arithmetic. Under heavy load [`PatSpatialEngineSmoke`](patterns.md#patspatialenginesmoke-kt-patspatialenginesmoke) has recorded the render thread
missing most of a window's blocks while **busy only a third of the elapsed time**; that run is in
`dev_docs/PAT_SPATIAL_MEASUREMENTS.md`. A thread that is idle two thirds of the time and still
misses its deadline is not a thread that needs faster code; it is a thread that is not being
scheduled.

Two things follow, and both are in the code rather than in advice:

- [`PatSpatialRoom.busyMsTotal`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt--patspatialroom--busymstotal) against elapsed time separates the two ways of falling behind.
  Near 100% busy with underruns means the work does not fit and this design is wrong. Far below
  it means the machine is oversubscribed, and [`PatSpatialEngineSmoke`](patterns.md#patspatialenginesmoke-kt-patspatialenginesmoke) says so instead of failing.
- The ring is sized for the scheduler's stalls, not for this code's, which is why it defaults to
  341 ms rather than the ~40 ms the arithmetic alone would justify.

Raising the render thread's priority was tried and reverted; the comment in
`PatSpatialRoom.start` records what it did instead of helping.

### Where this is written up for a reader

`public/docs/pat_spatial.md` — the page that decides *whether* to use this, rather than how it
works. It carries the findings without the percentiles, plus the two things this file cannot
hold: [`PatSpatialSoundDocs`](audio.md#patspatialsounddocs-kt-patspatialsounddocs)' published clips of the mono source, and the argument for why the
spatialised output has no clip and cannot have one. It is also declared in [`SoundPathMap`](audio.md#soundpathmap-kt-soundpathmap) as the
`pat-spatial` path, which is what keeps that page and this file from drifting apart.

## PatSpatialBudgetProbe.kt { #patspatialbudgetprobe-kt }

The `patSpatial` test that measures rather than asserts: Dough engines and Steam Audio effects in
a tight loop, with no room, no ring and no audio thread.

[`PatSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#patspatialsmoketest-kt-patspatialsmoketest), [`HeadTrackedSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatialsmoketest-kt-headtrackedspatialsmoketest) and [`PatSpatialEngineSmoke`](patterns.md#patspatialenginesmoke-kt-patspatialenginesmoke) all render
through [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom) and check the samples that came out. This one takes the arithmetic out
of that design and times it alone: [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine)s driven straight, for one, two and four
sources, against the milliseconds of audio a single block holds.

It asserts nothing: the test entry that runs it checks the exit code and one marker line, so
every figure it prints is one observation on one machine rather than a contract.
`dev_docs/PAT_SPATIAL_MEASUREMENTS.md` keeps the last set alongside the method that produced it.

The run drops the first tenth of its blocks as warmup, splits the per-block cost into its Dough
and Steam Audio halves, and reports the median, p99, p99.9 and the worst block, because those
move differently under load.

Run it with `tools/run_field_tests.py --id synth.pat-spatial.budget`.
