## PatSpatialEngineSmoke.kt { #patspatialenginesmoke-kt }

The delivery check on `patSpatial`: the only one of its tests that opens an audio device.

[`PatSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#patspatialsmoketest-kt-patspatialsmoketest) and [`HeadTrackedSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatialsmoketest-kt-headtrackedspatialsmoketest) pull [`PatSpatialBank`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialbank) themselves, which
proves the audio is right and says nothing about whether it reaches an output. This registers the
launch with [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) and lets that engine's own thread drain [`PatSpatialRing`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialring) for four
seconds.

Two outcomes end the run green having proved nothing, and telling them apart is why a silent
control patch is registered alongside the launch. `outputActive` false means no device opened.
`outputActive` true with the control patch never rendered means a device opened and is not
advancing: the engine refills its buffers only as OpenAL reports them processed, so a contended
device leaves it rendering no patch at all while still reporting an active output. Each case
names itself on stdout.

An underrun is not read as a failure on its own either. The run records the render thread's own
busy time and the machine's load average, and accepts an underrun only when that thread was well
short of saturating a core on a machine carrying far more load than it has cores.

Run it with `tools/run_field_tests.py --id synth.pat-spatial.engine`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/PatSpatialEngineSmoke.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/PatSpatialEngineSmoke/)

## PatSpatialSmokeTest.kt { #patspatialsmoketest-kt }

The audio check on `patSpatial`, run without an audio device: patterns that differ only in a
spatial tag, and the samples that came out of each.

This file and [`HeadTrackedSpatialSmokeTest`](patterns.md#headtrackedspatialsmoketest-kt-headtrackedspatialsmoketest) both pull [`PatSpatialBank`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialbank) themselves and compare
captures against each other rather than against remembered levels, which is what lets them run on
a machine with no sound card. [`PatSpatialEngineSmoke`](patterns.md#patspatialenginesmoke-kt-patspatialenginesmoke) covers the half they cannot reach, and
[`PatSpatialBudgetProbe`](patterns.md#patspatialbudgetprobe-kt-patspatialbudgetprobe) measures what a block costs.

Of the six spatial tags `patSpatial` reads, `az`, `dist`, `occl` and `spat` each get a case here;
`elev` and `air` get none. The remaining cases cover polyphony inside one source, `turnListener`,
and whether the ring absorbed the render thread's worst block.

Run it with `tools/run_field_tests.py --id synth.pat-spatial.smoke`.

## PatSynth.kt { #patsynth-kt }

A pattern on the audio seam: `pat(...)` driving Field's own voices in realtime.

[Making a sound in Field](../sound_paths.md) divides everything that makes
samples by one signature, `render(outL, outR, numFrames, ctx)`, and a path on that seam composes
with every other path on it. [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) is not on it: it is a free function that returns a
whole buffer, because a pattern has to be *queried* over an arc and there is no "next 128 frames"
to ask it for without a scheduler. This file is that scheduler, for Field's own voices.

Three parts, split by where they run:

| | where it runs | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`PatSynthFeeder`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthfeeder) | a daemon thread | queries the pattern a cycle at a time and turns events into frame-stamped [`PatSynthNote`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthnote)s |
| [`PatSynthBank`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthbank) | the audio thread | starts a note on the frame it was given, and synthesises |
| [`PatSynthLaunch`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthlaunch) | neither | owns both, and closes both |

Querying a pattern allocates, and a cycle of a large composed pattern is not a 2.67 ms job, so the
query cannot be on the audio thread. It does not have to be: what it produces is *frames*, and
being 400 ms early is the same sound as being exactly on time. The audio thread's remaining job is
an integer comparison. [`FaustPatternFeeder`](synthesis.md#faustpattern-kt-faustpatternfeeder) splits the work the same way for a Faust voice bank,
and the two are deliberate siblings.

### One voice, and the `.wav` that records it

One oscillator, one exponential-decay envelope, one one-pole lowpass, reading the same `gain`,
`pan`, `cutoff`, `sustain`, `note` and `speed` annotations off each event and using the same
`patDrumHz` map for unpitched atoms as [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) does.

What makes a `.wav` on a documentation page a record of the realtime path rather than a second
implementation of it is [`patSynthRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynthrenderstereo): it drives *this* bank through a [`SynthContext`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-synthcontext)
block by block, the way [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) does, and returns what came out. No audio device is
involved and nothing is re-derived.

### The output is the same at any block size

A scheduler that rounded each note to a block boundary would sound fine and be wrong, and the
symptom is that its output changes when the engine's buffer size does. [`patSynthRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynthrenderstereo) takes
`blockFrames`, and `PatSynthDocs` renders three bars at 64, 128, 512 and 1024 and asserts the four
buffers are bit-identical. That is the property that makes this a scheduler rather than a
quantiser.

The mixing loop runs samples outside and voices inside, and that is what makes the property exact
rather than close. The other way round, every note due in a block starts before any voice in that
block has finished, so which slot a note lands in moves with the block boundaries and so does the
order its samples are summed in; float addition is not associative, and a sixteen-voice bar reads
one ULP apart at two buffer sizes. Deciding starts and ends per sample costs one branch per voice
per sample.

## PatSynthDocs.kt { #patsynthdocs-kt }

The scenes and the checks for [`patSynth`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynth), the pattern scheduler that sits on the audio seam.

Every `.wav` here comes out of [`patSynthRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynthrenderstereo), which drives a real [`PatSynthBank`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthbank) through a
[`SynthContext`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-synthcontext) block by block exactly as [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) would. So these files are a record of
the realtime path with no audio device attached, rather than a second implementation of it.

### Three properties of the scheduler

**Block size does not change the output.** The same bar rendered at 64, 128, 512 and 1024 frames
per block comes back bit-identical. A scheduler that started each note at the top of the block it
fell in would pass every level and onset check here, and fail this one.

**The seam voice is the offline voice.** [`patRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsounddocs-kt--patrenderstereo) and [`patSynthRenderStereo`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynthrenderstereo) render the
same bar to the same onset counts and the same levels, but not to the same bytes: the offline
renderer works in seconds and truncates, this one works in frames and rounds, so a note can
differ by a frame at each end and a dense passage by a few merged onsets.

**The band analysis separates a kick from a hat.** [`BandSplit`](audio.md#bandanalysis-kt-bandsplit) over a kick-only render and a
hat-only render has to order its low and high bands opposite ways round. That is the smallest claim
that says the filters are filtering, and it is the property anything driving a display off
[`BandSplit`](audio.md#bandanalysis-kt-bandsplit) rests on.

## PatTranscription.kt { #pattranscription-kt }

Recovered audio, written back out as notation Field can re-render.

`public/docs/audio_render_analysis.md` draws the loop: notate, render, analyse, revise. This file is
the last arrow. Given a rendered buffer it returns a `pat("…")` string and the `PatPattern` it
parses to, so the output of analysis is the same kind of object as the input to synthesis and the
loop closes without a human in the middle of it. It is Field's only mini-notation printer, in
either direction; `PatEvent.sourceSpan` hands back the substring that *produced* an event, which is
the opposite problem.

**What is recoverable and what is not.** A step grid is recoverable from onsets; a *cycle* length is
not. Eight notes a beat apart are equally well "eight steps in one cycle at 0.5 cps" and "four steps
per cycle over two cycles at 1 cps", and no amount of listening distinguishes them, because the two
render to identical samples. So [`patTranscribe`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--pattranscribe) recovers the grid, makes the one arbitrary choice it
has to (one cycle, however many steps it found), and reports the [`PatTranscription.cps`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--pattranscription--cps) that makes
that choice sound right. What comes back is faithful to the audio rather than to the authoring
decision that produced it.

**A rest and a refusal are different, and mini-notation cannot say so.** `~` means "nothing sounds
here". There is no token for "something sounds here and a monophonic detector will not pretend to
name it". So a span whose harmonic residual says chord is dropped from [`PatTranscription.notes`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--pattranscription--notes) into
[`PatTranscription.declined`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--pattranscription--declined), appears in the emitted string as `~`, and is named explicitly in
[`PatTranscription.warnings`](patterns.md#pattranscription-kt--pattranscription--warnings). So the notation is what the detector will stand behind and the
warnings are the rest of what it heard.

## PatTranscriptionCorpus.kt { #pattranscriptioncorpus-kt }

A corpus that scores a transcription against the notation that generated the audio.

The ground truth here costs nothing and is exact. Transcription research is normally bounded by
annotation: someone listens to a recording, writes down what they think is in it, and the
transcriber is measured against a human's opinion. Field authored the notation, rendered it through
its own synthesiser, and still has the notation, so the reference is the audio's cause rather than
a reading of it. Every number in [`PatTranscriptionCorpus`](patterns.md#pattranscriptioncorpus-kt-pattranscriptioncorpus) is a comparison against that.

[`referenceOf`](patterns.md#pattranscriptioncorpus-kt--pattranscriptioncorpus--referenceof) therefore mirrors [`patSynthNotesForArc`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt--patsynthnotesforarc), which `patRenderStereo` schedules through,
rather than reimplementing the schedule: same events, same sort, same
`arc.start · secondsPerCycle`, same `Math.round` onto frames for the start and the hold, and no
`hasOnset` filter, because the renderer has none either. A reference computed from what the schedule
*ought* to be would be measuring this file's understanding of the renderer instead of the detector.

**Half the corpus is designed to fail.** A harness that only contains material its detector handles
measures the tuning rather than the range. So there is a legato line
with no attacks in it, a triad a monophonic detector must refuse rather than name, a line fast enough
to sit under the analysis window, a noise train with no pitch in it at all, and square and sawtooth
timbres whose harmonic stacks are the classic octave-error traps. What each case is *for* is written
into [`PatTranscriptionCase.purpose`](patterns.md#pattranscriptioncorpus-kt--pattranscriptioncase--purpose) and printed with its score, so a regression shows up as a
sentence rather than a delta.

The `*-untold` cases exist to measure one design claim rather than assert it: that telling the
detector the register it is listening to — the same contract `patDetectOnsetSamples` has with
`minGapSeconds` — is worth more than any threshold. The pair differs in nothing but whether
`minHz`/`maxHz` come from the notation or from the wide default.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/PatTranscriptionCorpus.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/PatTranscriptionCorpus/)

## PatTranscriptionGallery.kt { #pattranscriptiongallery-kt }

The figure that makes the round trip something you look at rather than read about.

One panel per case, one shared MIDI axis, and the two note sets drawn on top of each other: the
notation Field authored as a hollow outline, and what the detector heard as a solid bar inside it.
Agreement is then a filled outline and disagreement is a bar with nothing around it or an outline with
nothing in it — which is the whole reason to overlay rather than stack. A stacked pair of piano rolls
asks the reader to compare two pictures; an overlay asks them to spot the exceptions.

Drawn as SVG strings into a `StringBuilder`, following `PatPianoRollGallery` exactly, including its
palette. Same reasons: a piano roll is line art, and a diffable figure shows a changed detector as a
changed rectangle rather than as a changed PNG blob. No AWT, no browser, no GPU, no Field window.

The F0 trace is drawn on the same axis as the notes, because it is in the same units, and it is the
part of the figure that shows *why* a note was missed: a trace wandering between two outlines is a
straddling window, and a trace that vanishes is the voicing gate closing. Neither is visible in a
score table.

## Sequencing.kt { #sequencing-kt }

Notes with times on them, and a lazy player for a stream of them. [`ScheduledNote`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-schedulednote) is the event,
`noteProcess { … }` turns a suspending block into a [`NoteProcess`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-noteprocess), and a [`NoteProcess`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-noteprocess) draws itself
as a piano roll.

Time is in seconds and pitch is a MIDI number, fractional wherever you want it, with
[`midiToFrequency`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt--miditofrequency) and [`frequencyToMidi`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt--frequencytomidi) to cross between the two. Inside the block the receiver is
a [`NoteSequenceScope`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-notesequencescope) carrying a cursor, so consecutive `note(…)` calls lay themselves out end to
end and `rest(…)` leaves a gap.

The block is a generator rather than a list, which is what makes `while (true)` a legitimate way to
write a sequence: a [`NoteProcess`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-noteprocess) pulls from it only as far as the window it is asked about, keeps
a few seconds of what has already gone past, and drops the rest. Moving the playhead is what
unrolls more.

Nothing here makes a sound. A [`NoteProcess`](patterns.md#sequencing-kt-noteprocess) is a structure to read notes out of and to look at;
`TidalPatterns.kt` is the other way to write one, and the synthesis category is what plays it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Sequencing.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Sequencing/)

**Used in:** [Boolean network music examples](../boolean_network_music_examples.md), [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md)

## TidalPatterns.kt { #tidalpatterns-kt }

Field's pattern language: a compact text notation for musical structure, an exact algebra over
cycles, and a scheduler that turns the result into events in seconds.

`pat("bd [hh hh] sd")` parses, the combinators on [`PatPattern`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patpattern) transform, and `scheduled(…)`,
`respond(…)` and `asNotes(…)` are the three ways out. The middle stage is exact: a query asks a
pattern about a [`PatArc`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patarc), a half-open span of [`PatQ`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patq) rational cycles, so a third of a bar sped up,
reversed and slowed down again lands where it started. Seconds appear only at the boundary, and
`cps` is where that conversion happens.

The notation follows Tidal in style rather than to the letter, and an atom is any string rather
than a sample name, so a pattern can drive a synth voice, a property, an OSC send or a box launch
as readily as a drum. The Field-facing API stays small and biased toward generic event streams
rather than toward drum machines or sample triggers.

The design split is:

- parse short textual pattern expressions with `pat("...")`
- keep transforms exact in rational cycle space using `PatQ` / `PatArc`
- expose scheduled events in seconds at the public boundary
- allow atoms to mean anything, not just instruments or samples
- bridge easily into the existing note-process / piano-roll system
- also launch directly as a generic side-effecting event source

Read the surface from the outside in:

1. Parse:

        val hats = pat("bd [hh hh] sd")

2. Transform in cycle space:

        val varied = pat("a b c d")
            .every(4) { it.rev() }
            .sometimes { it.fast(2) }

        val layered = stack(
            pat("bd ~ sd"),
            pat("[hh hh hh hh]").degradeBy(0.2)
        )

    Simultaneous events (chords in music contexts):

        val triad = pat("c, e, g")     // All three fire at once during the same beat
        val voicing = pat("<c e g>, <g b d>")  // Pick one set per cycle, stacked

    Arpeggiate over a chord or note sequence:

        val bassArp = pat("bass bass bass").arp(60, 64, 67, speed = 4) // C major chord, 4 steps
        val upAndDown = pat("pad").arp(listOf("C3", "E3", "G3"), mode = ArpMode.UPDOWN, speed = 8)
        val randomArp = pat("keys").arp(48, 50, 52, 55, 57, mode = ArpMode.RANDOM, seed = 42)

3. Schedule into seconds:

        val events = pat("kick <snare rim>")
            .scheduled(cps = 2.0, startAt = 1.5)
            .take(8)
            .toList()

        events.first().start
        events.first().duration

    Or align directly to a shared musical clock:

        val master = musicClock()
        val sixteenth = master.subdivide(4.0)
        val upcoming = pat("bd [hh hh] sd")
            .scheduled(cps = 0.5, clock = sixteenth)
            .take(8)
            .toList()

    Euclidean suffixes attach directly to the preceding event or subgroup:

        val groove = pat("[bd cp](3,8) hh!2")

    A `k` or `g` in the same brackets asks for a Kolakoski figure over that many steps instead —
    `k` for the self-describing run-length reading, `g` for the gaps one. See PatKolakoski.kt:

        val selfDescribing = pat("bd(k16) hh*4")
        val dense = pat("bd(g16,3)")

    Repetition and density are distinct:

        val replicated = pat("bd!2 cp")
        val densified = pat("bd*2 cp")

    Elongation holds an event across later steps:

        val held = pat("superpiano@3 superpiano")

    Curly-brace polymeters can also take an explicit subdivision:

        val polymeter = pat("{bd hh 808:4}%8")
        val layeredPolymeter = pat("{bd sd stab, cp arpy cr arpy}")

    Inside square brackets, `|` picks one alternative per cycle:

        val randomChoice = pat("[bd*4|hh*12|cp*2]")

    Atom names can still carry sample-style parameter payloads:

        val parameterized = pat("bd:(1,2,3) hh")

    By default, `scheduled(...)`, `respond(...)`, `respondAhead(...)`, and
    `asNotes(...)` use the ambient `PatClock` from box context if one exists,
    otherwise they fall back to `musicClock()`. Pass `clock = null` if you
    want a zero-based schedule instead.

4. Map atoms into existing note processes:

        val bass = pat("0 3 5 7").asNotes(cps = 2.0) { event ->
            val degree = event.value.toIntOrNull() ?: return@asNotes emptyList()
            listOf(
                note(
                    pitch = 36 + degree,
                    duration = event.duration * 0.95,
                    start = event.start,
                    label = event.value
                )
            )
        }

5. Or respond directly, without assuming anything about the atom:

        pat("flash spin fade").respond(cps = 1.0) { event ->
            box.display("atoms", "${event.value} @ ${event.start}")
        }

    If you want callback time slightly before event time, use lookahead:

        pat("flash spin fade").respondAhead(ahead = 0.05, clock = musicClock()) { event ->
            box.display("atoms", "${event.value} in ${event.start - now}")
        }

    Scheduled events also retain the source span of the atom that produced
    them, so live debug tools can point back into the pattern text:

        pat("bd [hh hh] sd").respond(cps = 2.0) { event ->
            __m("pat").patHighlight(event)
        }

You can also map the parsed atom text immediately:

       data class Cue(val color: String, val gain: Float)

       val cues = pat("calm bright danger") { atom ->
           when (atom) {
               "calm" -> Cue("#0af", 0.15f)
               "bright" -> Cue("#fff", 0.4f)
               else -> Cue("#f80", 0.8f)
           }
       }

Important units and expectations:

- `start`, `end`, and `duration` on scheduled events are in seconds.
- `cps` still means cycles per second; that is the conversion boundary from
  cycle space into scheduled real time.
- Most pattern combinators are pure transforms over cycle queries.
- `respond(...)` is a coroutine event driver. `respondAhead(...)` lets the
  callback see future events before their target `start`.
- `asNotes(...)` is the memoized bridge when you want the same future schedule
  to drive playback logic and piano-roll inspection without recomputing it.

Three companion files extend this one. Read them before writing a `map { }`, because one of them
probably already has the combinator:

- `PatSignals.kt` — continuous/signal patterns (`sine`, `saw`, `perlin`, `rand`) and the
  discretisers that turn them back into events (`segment`, `struct`, `range`, `quantise`).
- `PatAlgebra.kt` — how two patterns of different types meet, and whose rhythm survives
  (`|+|` / `|+` / `+|`, `#`, and named parameters via `with(gain(...), pan(...))`).
- `PatComposition.kt` — arrangement (`off`, `superimpose`, `jux`, `iter`, `linger`, `randcat`,
  `shuffle`) and pitch (`scale`, `chords`, `voiceLead`).

`respond(...)` and `respondAhead(...)` are the hooks that assume nothing about the atom: it can
drive a synth voice, a visual, a property, an OSC send, a sample or a box launch. `pat(...)` is the
name to write against, and the one that will survive if the language underneath it changes.

### PatExprContext { #tidalpatterns-kt-patexprcontext }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">PatExprContext</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/TidalPatterns/#L1709)

Thread-local context for evaluating `{{...}}` expressions inside patterns. Expression bodies can read [`cycle`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt--patexprcontext--cycle) (0-based cycle index) and [`t`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt--patexprcontext--t) (fractional position inside the queried arc, 0.0..1.0).
